title: Grade 7 Science — Wed, Jun 18
description: Nutrition in Plants — Day 3 of 5: Parasitic, saprotrophic, and insectivorous plants
subject: science

questions.question: Cuscuta (dodder) is an example of which type of plant?
questions.explanation: Cuscuta is a parasitic plant — it lacks chlorophyll and wraps around host plants, absorbing food and nutrients from them.

questions.question: Parasitic plants like Cuscuta use special structures called ___ to absorb food from the host.
questions.explanation: Cuscuta develops haustoria — root-like structures that penetrate the host plant's stem to absorb water and nutrients.

questions.question: Which of the following is an insectivorous plant?
questions.explanation: Venus flytrap is an insectivorous plant — it traps and digests insects to obtain nitrogen in nitrogen-poor soils.

questions.question: Why do insectivorous plants trap insects?
options: To obtain nitrogen, which is scarce in their soil
questions.explanation: Insectivorous plants can photosynthesize, but they live in nitrogen-deficient soil. They trap insects to supplement their nitrogen supply.

questions.question: Organisms that obtain nutrition by breaking down dead and decaying matter are called:
questions.explanation: Saprotrophs (like fungi and some bacteria) obtain nutrition by breaking down dead and decaying organic matter, releasing nutrients back into the environment.

questions.question: Mushrooms are an example of:
questions.explanation: Mushrooms are fungi — they are saprotrophs. They secrete digestive enzymes onto dead organic matter, absorb the digested nutrients.

questions.question: The pitcher plant (Nepenthes) catches insects using:
options: A pitcher-shaped modified leaf with digestive fluid
questions.explanation: The pitcher plant has pitcher-shaped modified leaves that contain digestive fluid. Insects fall in and are digested.

questions.question: Cuscuta is yellowish-orange in colour because:
options: It absorbs orange pigments from its host
questions.explanation: Cuscuta lacks chlorophyll (the green pigment), which is why it appears yellowish-orange. Without chlorophyll it cannot photosynthesize.

questions.question: The relationship in parasitic nutrition is:
questions.explanation: Parasitic nutrition is a type of symbiosis where the parasite benefits at the expense of the host, which is harmed.

questions.question: Saprotrophic organisms are important for the ecosystem because they:
options: Return nutrients from dead matter back to the soil
questions.explanation: Saprotrophs decompose dead organic matter and recycle nutrients (like nitrogen and carbon) back into the soil, making them available for plants.

questions.question: Which nutrient do insectivorous plants mainly get from insects?
questions.explanation: Insects are rich in proteins, which provide nitrogen. Insectivorous plants trap insects mainly to supplement their nitrogen supply.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an insectivorous plant?
questions.explanation: Cuscuta is a parasitic plant (not insectivorous). Venus flytrap, Sundew, and Pitcher plant are all insectivorous.

questions.question: Bread mould (Rhizopus) is an example of:
questions.explanation: Bread mould (Rhizopus) is a saprotrophic fungus that grows on dead organic matter like stale bread.

questions.question: The Sundew plant (Drosera) traps insects using:
options: Sticky tentacle-like structures with sweet secretions
questions.explanation: Sundew plants have leaves covered in sticky, hair-like structures (tentacles) that secrete a sugary, sticky substance to trap insects.

questions.question: Which mode of nutrition do bacteria like Rhizobium follow?
questions.explanation: Rhizobium and many other soil bacteria are saprotrophic — they break down organic matter in the soil to obtain nutrition.
